articles.title: A warning of ‘breakdowns and deficiencies’ in security at the US central bank
articles.content: The Fed’s Office of Inspector General warned of potential security breaches at the US central bank © Reuters Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on x (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on facebook (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on linkedin (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on x (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on facebook (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on linkedin (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Abigail Hauslohner in Washington Published September 29 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page This is an on-site version of the White House Watch newsletter. You can read the previous edition here . Sign up for free here to get it on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Email us at [email protected] Hello from Washington and welcome to White House Watch. Here’s what we’re looking at today: Federal Reserve’s watchdog warns of security “deficiencies” at central bank Marco Rubio blames a “foreign actor” for the UK terror plot over the weekend US completes withdrawal of troops from Iraq The Federal Reserve’s watchdog has warned of “breakdowns and deficiencies” in security at the US central bank after a departing official was suspected of removing sensitive information, highlighting vulnerabilities at the institution. The Fed’s Office of Inspector General flagged potential breaches by an unnamed employee in the international finance division, culminating in 279 “data loss prevention” alerts in the 90 days before they retired in July 2024, 111 of these potentially involved information relating to the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee and 40 potentially contained central bank material. “This potential incident highlighted information security risks and control breakdowns and deficiencies that we believe require the board’s immediate attention,” the watchdog wrote in a report released on Monday. Government officials have long harboured concerns about the security of the Fed, which is seen as a high-value target for foreign adversaries because of the board’s proprietary financial information. The watchdog recommended tighter security procedures, which the Fed agreed to implement, but it said there was insufficient basis to pursue a misconduct investigation into the matter. What’s next for the global economy? Economics leader writer Tej Parikh and European economics commentator Martin Sandbu will be answering questions on the next stage of growth, its biggest risks and how global businesses and households will be affected. Submit your question here for the latest instalment of Ask an Expert happening on Thursday October 1. The latest headlines US secretary of state Marco Rubio said a “foreign actor” was involved in a suspected terrorist plot near a British air force base this weekend, in remarks that will intensify global scrutiny of the incident . The US Treasury on Monday took its first concrete steps towards cracking down on a suite of strategies used by wealthy US investors to cut their tax bills . Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece has caused a political stir in Romania after suggesting the US could bring down governments. Trump asked Xi Jinping if China wanted to buy American weapons , US envoy says. Private equity has become an important target on the campaign trail for the US midterms as candidates blame large investors for soaring housing costs . Divisions within Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again movement risk damaging Republicans ahead of the midterm elections. What we’re hearing Happening under the radar this week: the US is completing the withdrawal of most of its forces from Iraq. You would be forgiven for thinking: ‘Didn’t this already happen?’ Yes, it did, in 2011. US forces returned to fight the Islamic State a few years later. And now, 23 years after the initial US invasion of Iraq, nearly all US troops are expected to withdraw from the country by tomorrow. Kurdish leaders in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region of Iraq’s north are unhappy. Masrour Barzani tells my colleague Mehul Srivastava that the Americans are leaving their Kurdish allies without any missile defences and vulnerable to Iranian attack amid a war started by Donald Trump six months ago. “The threat is real,” Barzani said in a recent interview. The abandonment by Washington is “shameful”. Could you be the FT’s next stock picking champion? The FT’s new Stock Picking Game is a fast, fun way to test your trading instincts, sharpen your market expertise and compete for the chance to win £1,000. Terms and conditions apply. Register for season two now. Viewpoints Democrats are likely to make gains in Congress in November’s midterm elections but a divided government is unlikely to derail Trump’s agenda , argues Edward Luce. Jonathan Derbyshire says that, although Republicans are outspending the Democrats by around $1bn to $750mn, they are heading for a historic defeat. For once, the Fed has put Main Street before Wall Street, writes Sheila Bair US accounting editor Stephen Foley highlights how requirements under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act are being rolled back. Your browser does not support playing this file but you can still download the MP3 file to play locally. Recorded in front of an audience at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, host Lucy Fisher and political editor George Parker unpack Andy Burnham’s first conference speech as prime minister. From rethinking Britain’s relationship with the EU to ending the pensions triple lock and scrapping the electoral system, Burnham laid out an ambitious agenda for the country. Lucy and George speak to business secretary Jonathan Reynolds about the prime minister’s plans, before northern correspondent Jennifer Williams and Inside Politics writer and columnist Stephen Bush join them to give their takeaways from the week. articles.content: Inflation and interest rates tracker: see how your country compares on x (opens in a new window) Inflation and interest rates tracker: see how your country compares on facebook (opens in a new window) Inflation and interest rates tracker: see how your country compares on linkedin (opens in a new window) Inflation and interest rates tracker: see how your country compares on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Inflation and interest rates tracker: see how your country compares on x (opens in a new window) Inflation and interest rates tracker: see how your country compares on facebook (opens in a new window) Inflation and interest rates tracker: see how your country compares on linkedin (opens in a new window) Inflation and interest rates tracker: see how your country compares on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Valentina Romei , Alan Smith and Janina Conboye in London Published November 30 2021 Updated September 30 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Stay informed with free updates Simply sign up to the Global Economy myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox. Jump to section Country-by-country overview Policy rate decisions How inflation swept the world Latest CPI figures Central bank policy rates CPI by component Energy costs Interest rate expectations House prices The FT global inflation and interest rates tracker provides a regularly updated picture of consumer price inflation and central bank policy rates around the world. Our tracker features the latest inflation and policy rate data for most countries, historical figures, as well as key factors affecting policymakers’ decisions on borrowing costs. Bookmark this page to keep up to date as the global inflation story evolves. Country-by-country overview Many central banks have been lowering borrowing costs as global inflation gradually eases from the multi-decade highs recently recorded in many countries. Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings. While inflation in most nations has come down from its peak, many policymakers have warned that the last leg of the journey to central banks’ target — which in most advanced economies is 2 per cent — will be the hardest. [Back to top] Policy rate decisions This chart shows the outcome of central bank decisions since the pandemic, when many policymakers moved to lower borrowing costs. Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings. Higher borrowing costs helped ease the fast pace of price growth that swept the world during the pandemic, but many countries have now entered a fresh cycle of lowering rates. [Back to top] How inflation swept the world Entering the pandemic, inflation rates in many advanced economies were at or near the two per cent target level. But that changed, as this global animation shows. Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings. Post-pandemic supply chain disruptions and rising energy prices resulting from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine triggered a wave of inflation that left few countries untouched. [Back to top] Latest CPI figures This chart allows you to compare consumer price index figures for any three countries. Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings. Data in this chart is updated regularly following key releases from national statistics offices. [Back to top] Central bank policy rates This chart allows you to compare borrowing costs for up to three countries. Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings. Data in this chart is updated regularly following central bank policy decisions. [Back to top] CPI by component The latest figures for the world’s largest economies show that core inflation, a key measure of underlying price pressures that excludes food and energy, remains elevated in many G7 countries. Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings. [Back to top] Energy costs A rise in energy prices was the main driver of inflation in many countries in recent years, but gas and electricity costs have retreated from their peaks during the energy crisis that followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings. [Back to top] Interest rate expectations The yields on 2-year government bonds are strongly affected by market expectations of interest rates over that time. Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings. [Back to top] House prices The cost of homes soared in many countries during the pandemic, but high mortgage rates have led to a slowdown in house price growth in a number of countries. Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings. articles.title: An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich
articles.content: An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on x (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on facebook (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on linkedin (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on whatsapp (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on x (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on facebook (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on linkedin (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Jessica Salter . Photography by Joël Hunn Published September 30 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. I moved to Zürich from Geneva when I was four, but I was born in Munich. (My mother is Dutch and my father is German.) I moved back to Germany in my early teens, but I returned here to study economics at the University of St Gallen before completing another degree in economics and philosophy at Harvard. Now I split my time between London and Zürich, working in finance and investments along with writing and performing poetry. I feel very Swiss. Our first home was an apartment near Lake Zürich. But the home I really remember was further out in Schindellegi, a village that feels quite rural despite only being half an hour from the city centre. My childhood memories are mainly sensory: the mountains, the lake. Sound behaves very differently here than in most cities. You feel cocooned. The lake is central to life in Zürich ; when it’s warm, everyone gathers on the water’s edge at weekends and after work. I like sitting on the terrace at Alex Lake Zürich, a hotel right on the water (there’s a little boat that runs back and forth to Storchen, a hotel and restaurant in the city centre). On the northern shore, La Muña has a small rooftop terrace that’s perfect at sunset, with the whole city laid out below. A view of the Limmat river towards Lake Zürich © Joël Hunn Marktgasse in the city centre © Joël Hunn Having a treat there © Joël Hunn Everyone here is sporty and nearly everyone is a semi-professional cyclist. I’m not – I ride a Dutch bike with upright handlebars – and I prefer hiking to cycling. Üetliberg, a mountain just above the city, is the easiest hike; you can walk for a couple of hours. Etzel on the south side of Lake Zürich is a proper half-day walk and there’s a restaurant at the top. For a serious hike, I go to Grosser Mythen , a mountain with steep, hairpin turns. I have been going to Seebad Utoquai, the public baths on the promenade between Bellevue and Zürichhorn, since childhood. You can bathe in the lake too: people even swim to work with all their things in a waterproof bag. I’ve recently joined a group of female entrepreneurs who meet further down the lake towards Richterswil . We do a cold plunge in the lake, then help each other with business plans, funding and networking. On Römergrasse in the city centre © Joël Hunn At Dr Peter Bichsel Fine Books © Joël Hunn L’Alsace Heureuse by Hansi on display there © Joël Hunn People think Zürich is very straight-laced, and on the surface it is. But behind closed doors, it’s radically creative. There’s a thriving techno scene: Adriatique and Jenny Cara are based here. In my early 20s, I had a DJ friend who would take me to Kreis 5, which is a bit like London’s Shoreditch. Basel and Zürich are notorious for hating each other because of football, but people come here from Basel for the music; they respect each other’s techno scenes. One of the most beautiful buildings here is the Schweizerische Nationalbank, right in the centre on Börsenstrasse. There is a building next door, the SNB Forum, where you can see bank notes and explore the history of SNB on an interactive LED screen. It also hosts the Karl Brunner Distinguished Lecture Series; I’ve heard American economist John H Cochrane speak there. Growing up in Zürich has been influential in teaching me how a European capital of finance conducts itself. There’s a big focus on family-owned businesses here, so naturally they think about how to exist for many generations. In New York or London, where I’ve also lived and worked, the pace is more rapid, which can feel quite short-term. At the shop of Swiss label Lamarel © Joël Hunn I’ve always spent more money on books than clothes. Dr Peter Bichsel Fine Books in the heart of the old town is my favourite bookshop. It specialises in beautiful and rare books from the 15th to 21st centuries – I once found an early edition of one of Else Lasker-Schüler’s poetry collections – and the shop is a centre for literary minds and creatives. Zürich also has brilliant vintage furniture shops, such as Kioskio , which sources pieces from private collections across Europe; the prices are genuinely good. For clothes, I like Lamarel, a Swiss label built around simple, easy shapes. The city has different dress codes depending where you are: around the art schools and design studios in Kreis 4 and Kreis 5, the style is loose and vintage. In the centre it is more conservative, with muted tones and immaculate tailoring. Outside at Trattoria Neumarkt © Joël Hunn Eating a number of dishes there © Joël Hunn Green olives, stracciatella di burrata with chilli crunch and chive, and sourdough bread with miso butter © Joël Hunn The food scene has changed a great deal since I was a child. There used to be only a handful of restaurants serving international cuisine; now there are many. Amia is a new outdoor bar with a French Mediterranean-inspired menu, and I love the confit of char at Bürgli. Trattoria Neumarkt does rotating pop-up menus, often with a Japanese-Italian blend; I go for its Japanese take on cacio e pepe with udon noodles. My Italian partner was initially sceptical but has since been won over. When I want to write, I go to B2 Boutique Hotel, a former brewery near the Google offices that now has the most extraordinary library bar: books floor to ceiling, all the way round. I’ll sit there for hours with a coffee and write. But mostly I find myself going back to the lake. I go down to Bürkliplatz, a town square where you can sit right on the water. I find it endlessly inspiring. Zürich has taught me a sensitivity for atmosphere, silence and order. There’s a layer to the city that makes you attentive to what is not said, and that’s where poetry can happen. articles.title: What is Black design now?
articles.content: What is Black design now? on x (opens in a new window) What is Black design now? on facebook (opens in a new window) What is Black design now? on linkedin (opens in a new window) What is Black design now? on whatsapp (opens in a new window) What is Black design now? on x (opens in a new window) What is Black design now? on facebook (opens in a new window) What is Black design now? on linkedin (opens in a new window) What is Black design now? on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Charlene Prempeh . Photography by Niall Hodson Published October 6 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Charlene Prempeh, curator of The Nue Black Aesthetic : What does the exhibition title mean to you? Phoebe Collings-James: I think about it more as a question, about where we’re at, what’s going on, how everyone is feeling – who are we, and why are we doing the things we’re doing? Taiba Akhuetie: I think it’s an evolution of how we portray ourselves in society, of how we have been brought up in our culture and how we express ourselves differently, without taking away from our identity. Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings. Samuel Ross: It does definitely bring a sense of autonomy. The title made me think about the ability we now have to posit ourselves to the world, rather than the image of the Black in contemporary [culture] being told to us, [as it has been] over the past few hundred years. If we think back to our studies, I can’t remember hearing about any type of Black vernacular tied to design. We always had to frack for it. Now we’re able to have some control over it. And that in itself feels quite new. Ini Archibong: This is new. There’s a Black aesthetic. But isn’t it somewhat outside of our control by the simple naming of it the Black aesthetic? That means that somebody that’s not Black is putting us as “other”, right? CP: To me, it doesn’t feel like an external effect. The exhibition was inspired by two texts. The Black Arts Movement written by Larry Neal in 1968, rooted in civil rights, and Trey Ellis’s 1989 essay, The New Black Aesthetic . They are both by Black men coming from an African-American perspective. “Nue” here comes from the French term nuance; the conditioning is that the Black aesthetic now is one where we can take the time to look at very specific experiences of different individuals, and of the diaspora too. Nifemi Marcus-Bello: I think it’s us dictating our own vision of what the Black aesthetic looks like. Growing up, you pick up books about Africa, and they’re usually written by someone from Europe. This feels a lot more important because you are curating it. Above, from left: (top row) Saunders and Prempeh, (middle row) Akhuetie, Ross and Collings-James, (bottom row) Archibong and Marcus-Bello © Niall Hodson CP: There is an inherent contradiction in doing a show called The Nue Black Aesthetic while arguing that not enough attention has been paid to the complexities of individual Black designers. How do you feel about that? Bianca Saunders: It feels like this is the start of us breaking away from just being a category. TA: I do think we have to be careful of people always grouping us together. Even when someone introduces me, it’s, “She’s a really talented Black artist”, and that can be frustrating. Why can’t we just be artists and designers? When you’re white you don’t get that. You don’t get: “That’s a white designer from Copenhagen.” PCJ: There’s a political diversity too. There is massive diversity in how you achieve liberation or what you fight for, and that comes through in the way people choose to make art and design. IA: During the early part of the pandemic, [people] were searching out designers of colour in the industrial space to have us speak for all of us. I was like, “Yeah, I did a couple of good tables and now I’m talking for Black designers?” There might be things that unify us within the diaspora. I can connect to Nifemi on being Nigerian. I can connect to Samuel on being of African descent in white spaces. But everybody’s coming from wildly different perspectives. You can’t project that we’re gonna have some kind of codified image. Eno Chandelier, 2023, by Ini Archibong © Cecil Mathieu. Courtesy of Friedman Benda and Ini Archibong CP: Are there particular elements of Black design that you think should be celebrated? IA: As much as I want to shy away from being monolithic, I’d describe being of African descent as “we don’t have to count to dance” – I don’t need to sit down and calculate everything. I can just feel my way through it. And I get that feeling when I look at the work of other people of the diaspora. A lot of my commissions aren’t coming from people that are going to understand the animism and the mythology from my region of Nigeria that influenced the piece. But the energy is there, and they’re going to absorb that energy. It’s like it’s a gift from my culture to you and your home. TA: I think people often celebrate the more outlandish designs that you can visibly see are associated with Black culture, but it’s important to also show the subtlety in design and the freedom that Black people have to just design based on a leaf falling from the tree in Victoria Park, or my grandma’s chair in my house. BS: That’s interesting because I feel the work that is more subtle is what is getting people paid more – because then it relates to everyone. TA: But is it celebrated? I think your work is very subtle and chic, it’s beautiful, but that doesn’t take away from your Blackness at all. The Braided Shower Curtain, 2025, by Taiba Akhuetie © Objets Pointus Braided bench, by Taiba Akhuetie © Stephy Clark BS: You don’t have to relate to everyone, but people need to see themselves in your work, or have some sort of understanding of it, otherwise I don’t think it survives. NMB: But I think the beautiful thing about being Black and being a designer is that the approach to design is usually contextual. Most Black designers, I would say, are trying to tell the story of the now. IA: When I [first] started putting my work out there [in 2011], if anybody wanted to talk about my race I was like “I don’t talk to white people about race. That’s it. Look at the piece: it’s a good office table. It’s beautiful and it’s not square.” So when there did come a time when there was a spotlight, then for me personally it became important to start sharing some of the things that were inside me. It’s like, “you’re a Black designer” – then OK, let me talk to my Black people, let me talk to the people that are in school and let them know, “Hey, there’s a way to do this.” SR: It was a forming of sovereignty, actually. The important part was that Black designers could just speak to one another through their work at a very high level. Prempeh (front) with the six designers, from left: Collings-James, Archibong,  Marcus-Bello, Saunders, Akhuetie and Ross © Niall Hodson CP: Have you had moments when it felt like your work has been interpreted primarily through the fact that you’re Black? TA: In my work I use hair and braiding, and that is associated with Blackness. I am the artist and I am Black and that is inherent in my work. But I think that sometimes beyond that conversation, people don’t have much to say. NMB: During Black Lives Matter [in 2020], I said no to maybe five projects because I’m not African American, I don’t have the same experience. I was raised in Nigeria, I’ve lived in the UK for a while; I understand what it means to be Black, but the everyday struggle, I am only just learning. IA: Some journalists who were trying to ride the wave of being racially conscious [at that time] asked very unconscious and offensive questions. I’m like, “Why would I talk to you about my experience with police brutality? So you could sell more magazines?” BS: Being a Black designer, you have
